title: Links and joints
about: How a robot arm is built, how far it can reach, and how it works out its angles.

html: A robot arm is a chain of links and joints.

Links are the stiff parts, like the bones in your arm. Joints are where links connect and move, like your shoulder and elbow.
• Turning joints (engineers say revolute) rotate like a door hinge. A servo usually drives each one.
• Sliding joints (prismatic) move in a straight line, like a drawer.
Degrees of freedom
Each joint that can move on its own adds one degree of freedom. Two joints let an arm reach spots on a flat surface. To reach any spot in 3D and point its gripper in any direction, an arm needs six.
Your own arm has about seven, so you can keep your hand flat on a table and still move your elbow.
The simulator next has two links: an 18 cm upper arm and a 14 cm forearm.
Working backwards
In the simulator you picked joint angles and watched where the hand went. That's forward kinematics.
Robots usually need the opposite: "The block is here. What angles do I need?" That's inverse kinematics, and the robot's computer solves it with trigonometry.
Most spots can be reached two ways, elbow up or elbow down, like reaching for a cup with your elbow high or low.
And no arm reaches farther than its links laid end to end. Here that's 18 + 14 = 32 cm.

steps.q: A robot arm has an 18 cm link and a 14 cm link. What's the farthest its hand can reach from the shoulder?
steps.explain: Laid out straight, the links add up: 18 + 14 = 32 cm. Anything farther is out of reach.

steps.q: Which kind of joint moves in a straight line instead of turning?
steps.explain: A sliding joint moves in a line, like a drawer. A turning joint rotates, like a hinge.

steps.q: A robot knows where a block is and works out the joint angles to reach it. What's that called?
steps.explain: Working backwards from a target to the angles is inverse kinematics.
